summary: This unit teaches you to choose, use and look after the graduated measuring devices an electrician needs: tapes, rules, laser distance meters, calipers, micrometers, torque tools and gauges. You will learn to measure safely around electrical equipment, set out positions from a drawing, find conductor and cable sizes by measurement, and do the calculations that follow. At Level 3 you also check other people's measurements, keep the devices accurate and keep the records.

blocks.p: A **graduated measuring device** is any device with a marked scale or a digital read-out that gives a size as a number: a tape, a rule, a caliper, a micrometer, a laser distance meter, a torque screwdriver, an angle finder. Electricians measure all day: cable routes, box heights, light spacing, conductor sizes, conduit sizes, bend radii and terminal torque. A wrong measurement costs money (cable cut short, boxes reset after plastering) and can cost safety (an undersized conductor, a loose terminal).

This unit is for Level 3 trainees. You are expected to choose the right device for the accuracy the job needs, measure correctly, work out the results, check and coach others, and keep the Centre's or company's devices accurate and recorded.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job

Isolate and prove dead before measuring inside equipment, use non-conductive devices near live parts, work safely at height and with lasers.

Measure routes, rooms and heights correctly, and know what makes each device read wrongly.
Use scales and written dimensions, work from a datum and from finished floor level, and space fittings evenly.
Check them before use, hold them correctly and read vernier, dial and digital scales.
Measure diameters, work out cross-sectional areas, and name the nearest standard size.

Use torque, gap, depth and angle devices
Set and read torque tools, feeler gauges, depth gauges, levels and angle finders.
Write every reading with its unit and the device used, compare it with the tolerance, and check other people's work.
Clean, store and check devices, keep a register, and take faulty ones out of use.

ul: Drawings and the Centre's work use **metric units**: millimetres (mm) and metres (m). Conductor areas are in square millimetres (mm²).

Much of the material in Jamaican hardware stores comes from North America, so you will also meet **inches and feet**: cable in 50, 100, 250 and 500 ft coils, conduit and boxes in inch 'trade sizes', and conductor sizes in **AWG** (American Wire Gauge). You must be able to convert.

The electrical code used in Jamaica is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**, which gives many distances in both systems. Use the figures on the drawing and in the specification for the job.
Heat, humidity and salt air are hard on measuring devices. Section 9 covers care.

blocks.p: Read the sections in order and work through every example with a calculator. If you can, have a tape, a caliper and a micrometer beside you. Then try the practice test and read every explanation.

blocks.note: **Trade sizes are names, not measurements.** A '3/4 inch' conduit is not 19 mm on the outside or the inside: the name comes from an old standard. Metric conduit (20 mm, 25 mm) is named by its outside diameter. Before you buy fittings, glands or saddles, measure the real outside diameter, and do not mix inch and metric fittings.

blocks.p: The rule for choosing: the device's resolution must be **finer than the tolerance** of the job, but no finer than is practical. Nobody sets out box heights with a micrometer, and nobody checks a conductor's diameter with a tape.

blocks.p: Measuring feels harmless, which is why people get hurt doing it. The hazards are electric shock and arc flash from conductive devices near live parts, falls while stretching a tape at height, eye injury from lasers, and trips over tapes.

ul: Wherever you can, measure with the equipment **isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead** with a two-pole tester that you check on a proving unit before and after.
Remember that the **incoming (supply) side** of a board's main switch stays live when the switch is off. Keep hands and devices away from it.

A **steel tape or metal rule conducts**. It can bridge two live parts or a live part and earth, and a steel tape can spring back or buckle into a board when it is released. Never use one near exposed or possibly live parts.
Use a **non-conductive fibreglass tape** or folding rule there. Check that it is clean and dry and has no metal threads or metal end fittings that could touch live parts.
A metal rule wrapped in insulating tape is still a metal rule. It is not an insulated tool.
Calipers, micrometers and feeler gauges are metal. Use them only on conductors and equipment that are **disconnected or proved dead**.
Use a sound stepladder or a tower, set up properly, and do not over-reach to stretch a tape: move the ladder.
For ceiling heights and long spans, a laser distance meter used from the floor is often the safest method.
Do not hold a tape for a colleague while standing on furniture.

blocks.p: Laser distance meters and laser levels are usually **Class 2** lasers: low power, but the beam can still dazzle and may harm the eye if stared into.

ul: Never look into the beam, and never aim it at anyone's eyes, or at mirrors, glass and shiny surfaces that could reflect it into someone's face.
Tell other people in the room when a laser is in use.
Where you can, set a laser level so that its beam is not at the eye height of people sitting or standing nearby.
Switch it off when you are not measuring. Do not let anyone treat it as a toy.
Read the class and the warnings on the label, and follow the maker's instructions.

blocks.note: Keep tapes out of walkways and wind them in as soon as you have the reading. A tape stretched across a corridor in a school or shop is a trip hazard for people who are not expecting it.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Tapes, rules, laser meters and measuring wheels

ul: The **hook** at the end is loose on purpose. It slides by exactly its own thickness, so the tape reads correctly whether you hook it over an edge (pulling) or push it against a wall. A hook that is bent, or that no longer slides, or that slides too far, gives a wrong reading every time.
Read the tape **square on**, with your eye directly over the mark. Reading from one side gives **parallax error**.
Keep the tape **straight, flat and taut**. A tape that sags or bows follows a longer path than the straight line, so it **reads longer** than the true distance.
For an inside measurement between two walls, read the tape against the wall and add the length of the case if the maker marks it, or measure from each wall to a mark in the middle and add the two.
Check before use: the hook, the first 100 mm of the blade (the part that wears most), kinks and rust, and the lock.

blocks.p: Fibreglass tapes come in long lengths (20 m, 30 m, 50 m), do not conduct when clean and dry, and do not rust. They can **stretch** if pulled too hard and over the years, and they sag more than steel over a long span. Support a long fibreglass tape along the floor or a wall, pull it just taut, and check it against the reference tape from time to time.

A **folding rule** (often 2 m) folds into short hinged sections. It is stiff, so one person can measure up a wall or across a gap with it. Before use, check that the **joints are firm** and that it **opens out straight**: a loose or bent joint shortens or lengthens every reading. A wooden or fibreglass folding rule is useful near electrical equipment; one with metal joints and tips still needs care. A **steel rule** (150 mm or 300 mm) is for short, accurate marking out on the bench.

flow: Check the setting: does it measure from its front edge or its back edge?
Hold or rest the meter steady against the start point
Aim at a solid, matt target, square to the beam
Take the reading; repeat it once
Write it down with its unit

blocks.p: **Check a laser meter** by comparing it with a good tape over a known distance, such as 5 m and 10 m marked out in the workshop. Do this at set times and after any knock.

A **measuring wheel** (trundle wheel) is pushed along the ground and counts the distance on a counter. It is quick for long routes such as a trench line, a driveway or a boundary. It follows every bump and dip, slips on loose gravel and wet grass, and is not suitable for short or precise lengths. On rough ground, a long fibreglass tape laid along the route in stages is more reliable.

blocks.note: Take long measurements twice, ideally by two different methods, before you order expensive cable. A second reading costs a minute; a submain cut 2 m short costs the whole cable.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A scale of **1:50** means that 1 mm on the drawing stands for 50 mm in the building. **Real length = drawing length × scale number.** On a 1:20 drawing, 135 mm stands for 135 × 20 = 2,700 mm = 2.7 m. On a 1:200 site plan, 64 mm stands for 64 × 200 = 12,800 mm = 12.8 m.
A **scale rule** has edges marked for common scales (1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 1:200 and others), so you read real lengths directly. Check the scale in the drawing's title block and use the matching edge.

blocks.h: The limits of scaling a drawing

ul: **Written dimensions always win.** If a size is written on the drawing, use it; do not measure it.
If the drawing says **'Do not scale'**, use only the written dimensions, and ask the designer for any that are missing.
Photocopies, phone photos and prints 'reduced to fit' are **no longer to scale**. Check a print by measuring a dimension that is written on it, or the scale bar if there is one.
A plan does not show heights. It does not show the drops down walls, or the real route round beams and ducts.
Treat scaled lengths as an **estimate**. Check on site before you order a large amount.

blocks.p: Heights on drawings are given above **finished floor level (FFL)**, often written **AFFL** (above finished floor level). During first fix the floor is often bare concrete, with the tiles and their bedding still to come. If you measure from the bare slab, every box ends up too low by the thickness of the floor finish.

**Example.** Outlets are drawn at 400 mm AFFL. The floor will have 10 mm tiles on 20 mm of bedding: a 30 mm finish. Mark the outlets at 400 + 30 = **430 mm above the bare slab**. Always ask the builder for the finish thickness; do not assume it.

Choose one **datum**: a fixed point or line, such as a corner of the room, a centre line or a level line. Measure **every** position from it. If you measure each box from the last one, every small error is carried forward and added to the next: ten boxes each 2 mm out can leave the last one 20 mm out. This is called **cumulative error**.

To keep a row of boxes at one height round a room, mark a **level line**: set up a laser level (or use a spirit level and a chalk line) at a known height above FFL, then measure up or down from that line to each box with a tape. Floors are rarely level, so measuring up from the floor at each box gives a row that follows the floor's bumps.

The usual pattern for a row of lights is equal spaces between them and **half a space at each end wall**. Then: **spacing = room length ÷ number of lights**, and the first light is half a spacing from the wall.

**Example.** Four lights along an 8.4 m room: spacing = 8.4 ÷ 4 = 2.1 m. The first light is 1.05 m from the end wall, then 3.15 m, 5.25 m and 7.35 m, all measured from the same wall. Check: the last light is 8.4 − 7.35 = 1.05 m from the far wall.

flow: Check the drawing: scale, written dimensions, heights AFFL
Find out the floor finish thickness
Choose the datum and mark the centre lines
Mark a level line round the walls
Work out the spacing and mark each position from the datum
Check every mark against the drawing, with a second person
Only then fix or drill

blocks.p: A tolerance of ± 5 mm on a height of 1,200 mm means the work passes from 1,195 mm to 1,205 mm, with both limits included. A box at 1,207 mm must be reset. When the drawing gives no tolerance, ask: do not invent one.

blocks.note: Mounting heights come from the drawing and the specification. Where a figure is given in this kit, such as 400 mm for outlets or 1,200 mm for switches, it is an example only.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A caliper has outside jaws (for diameters and widths), inside jaws (for bores and slots) and a depth rod (for depths). A common workshop caliper reads to **0.02 mm**.

flow: Wipe the jaws clean and close them: the two zeros must line up
Close the jaws on the work with light, even pressure, square to it
Read the main scale: whole millimetres to the left of the vernier zero
Find the vernier line that lines up exactly with a main-scale line
Multiply its number by 0.02 mm and add it to the main-scale reading

blocks.p: **Example.** The vernier zero has passed 16 mm on the main scale, and the 21st vernier line is the one that lines up. Reading = 16 + (21 × 0.02) = 16 + 0.42 = **16.42 mm**. (On many calipers the vernier is numbered 0 to 10, so that you read the hundredths directly; count the lines if you are unsure.)

ul: A **digital caliper** shows the reading on a screen. Press ZERO with the clean jaws closed, check that it is set to **mm**, not inches, and replace a weak battery.
A **dial caliper** shows the fraction of a millimetre on a dial. Check that the needle reads zero with the jaws closed.

On soft work, such as a **cable sheath**, close the jaws only until they just touch. Squeezing makes the cable read small. Measure in two directions at right angles, because cables are often slightly oval, and use the larger figure for conduit and gland sizes.

blocks.p: A micrometer measures to **0.01 mm**. The work sits between the fixed **anvil** and the moving **spindle**. The **sleeve** (barrel) is marked in millimetres, with half-millimetre lines on the other side of the line. The **thimble** has 50 divisions; one full turn moves the spindle 0.5 mm, so each division is 0.01 mm. The **ratchet** on the end slips when the right measuring pressure is reached.

flow: Wipe the anvil and spindle faces clean
Close them gently with the ratchet and check the zero
Hold the micrometer by its frame
Place the work square between the faces
Turn the ratchet until it clicks two or three times
Read the sleeve, then add the thimble

head: On the sleeve
On the thimble
Reading
rows: 3 mm showing, no half-millimetre line after it
3 mm showing, and the half-millimetre line after it
0 mm showing, and the half-millimetre line after it

blocks.note: The most common micrometer mistake is missing the half-millimetre line, which makes the reading exactly 0.50 mm too small. Ask yourself whether the answer is sensible: a conductor that 'measures' 1.28 mm when it should be about 1.78 mm has probably lost its half millimetre.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: With clean faces closed by the ratchet, the micrometer should read 0.00 mm. If it does not, it has a **zero error**. Either adjust the zero with the small spanner supplied, as the maker says, or correct every reading:

head: Closed reading
Type of error
Correction
rows: +0.03 mm (thimble zero has not reached the line)
−0.02 mm (thimble zero has gone past the line)

blocks.p: The screw thread of a micrometer multiplies force. Turning the thimble hard by hand squeezes the work, strains the frame and gives a small reading; it also wears the thread. Different people squeeze by different amounts, so their readings differ. The ratchet gives everyone the same light pressure. As a team leader, if two people get different readings on the same conductor, have both re-measure the same spot while you watch their method, before you blame the device or average the figures.

blocks.note: Never clean measuring faces with emery cloth or a file, never use a micrometer as a clamp, and never spin it closed by swinging the frame. Each of these damages the faces or the thread.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Conductor and cable sizes from measurements

blocks.p: Cable should be identified from the marking printed on its sheath or insulation. When the marking is missing or worn, you can find a conductor's size by measuring it. Do this only on cable that is **disconnected from every supply**.

flow: Strip a short length without nicking the copper
Zero-check the micrometer
Measure the diameter with the ratchet, in two directions at right angles
Work out the area: π × d² ÷ 4
Compare with the nearest standard size and record it

blocks.p: **Example.** A solid conductor measures 2.76 mm. Area = 3.142 × 2.76 × 2.76 ÷ 4 = 3.142 × 7.618 ÷ 4 = **5.98 mm²**: a 6 mm² conductor.
If the two directions differ by more than a few hundredths of a millimetre, the conductor has been flattened or damaged where you measured. Measure again on an undamaged part.

Do **not** measure across the whole bundle: the gaps between the strands make it read too big. Count the strands, measure the diameter of **one strand**, work out its area, and multiply by the number of strands.
**Example.** A conductor has 7 strands, each 1.35 mm. One strand = 3.142 × 1.35 × 1.35 ÷ 4 = 1.43 mm². Seven strands = 7 × 1.43 = **10.0 mm²**: a 10 mm² conductor.

blocks.note: In Jamaica you will meet both metric (mm²) and AWG conductors, and they are **not** exact matches: 12 AWG is about 3.3 mm², between 2.5 and 4 mm². With AWG, a lower number is a thicker wire. A measured size tells you what the conductor is; its current rating still comes from the table for that cable type. If a result falls between standard sizes, measure again and ask your instructor.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: The overall diameter of a cable

blocks.p: Measure the outside of the whole cable (or of an insulated single conductor) with a caliper closed lightly. You need the overall diameter for three things: the gland or bush size, the minimum bend radius, and the space the cable takes in conduit or trunking.

Bent too tightly, a cable's insulation is stretched and its conductors strained. The maker gives a minimum inside bend radius as a multiple of the overall diameter, commonly somewhere between 4 and 8 times for ordinary cables and more for armoured ones. **Minimum radius = factor × overall diameter.** A 9.5 mm cable with a factor of 6 must not be bent tighter than 6 × 9.5 = 57 mm radius. Always use the maker's factor.

Cables may fill only part of a conduit, so they can be drawn in without damage and can lose their heat. The limit comes from the code or the specification: the NEC, for example, allows three or more conductors to fill **40%** of the conduit's inside area. Work out each cable's area from its **overall** diameter, add the areas together and compare the total with the allowed area.

**Example.** A conduit has an inside diameter of 16 mm. Its area = 3.142 × 16 × 16 ÷ 4 = 201 mm², and 40% of that is 80 mm². Three conductors each 4.2 mm overall: one = 3.142 × 4.2 × 4.2 ÷ 4 = 13.9 mm²; three = **41.6 mm²**. They fit, with room to spare.

When the maker or the specification gives a maximum spacing for clips or saddles, the number of spaces = run length ÷ spacing, rounded **up**, and the number of fixings is **one more** than the number of spaces, because there is a fixing at each end. A 3.6 m run with fixings no more than 400 mm apart: 3.6 ÷ 0.4 = 9 spaces, so 10 fixings.

blocks.h: How much cable is left, and how much to order

ul: Many cables have **metre marks** printed along the sheath. The length left on a drum is the difference between the mark at the outer end and the mark at the inner end.
Order length = measured route + drops + terminations, plus a waste allowance (often 10 to 20%). A 15.8 m route with 10% added: 15.8 × 1.10 = 17.4 m.
If the supplier sells in feet, convert at the end: 17.4 ÷ 0.3048 = 57 ft.

sections.title: Torque, gap, depth and angle devices

blocks.p: **Torque** is turning force. A terminal that is too loose has a high resistance and overheats; one that is too tight crushes the conductor, strips the thread or cracks the device. Makers print the right torque on the device or in its instructions, in **newton metres (N·m)** or, on North American equipment, in pound-inches (lb-in). Tightness cannot be judged reliably by feel: two people tightening 'by hand' rarely reach the same figure.

ul: Set the tool's scale to the stated figure, in the right unit. To convert, N·m = lb-in ÷ 8.85: a terminal marked 35 lb-in needs 35 ÷ 8.85 = 4.0 N·m.
Turn smoothly until the tool **clicks or slips**, then stop. Do not 'add a bit' by hand afterwards.
Use the tool for tightening only, never to undo tight screws.
Where the maker says so, wind an adjustable torque tool back to its lowest setting after use, so the spring is not left compressed.
A torque tool is a measuring device: it goes on the register and is checked at set times and after a drop.

blocks.p: Many outlets, switches, breakers and connectors have a **strip gauge** moulded into the body: a short groove or line that shows how much insulation to remove. Lay the conductor in it and mark the length. Too little bare copper and the screw clamps on insulation; too much and bare copper shows outside the terminal.

A set of **feeler gauges** is a fan of thin steel blades, each marked with its thickness (for example 0.05 mm to 1.00 mm). To measure a gap, find the thickest blade, or stack of blades, that slides in with a light drag. Electricians use them for the **air gap** between a motor's rotor and stator, checked at several points round the rotor, and for contact gaps where the maker gives a figure. The blades are steel: the machine must be isolated, locked off and proved dead.

The **depth rod** of a caliper, or a separate depth gauge, measures down from a surface: the depth of a chase before the conduit goes in, how far a box is recessed behind the plaster line, or the depth of a blind hole. Rest the base flat on the surface and read as usual.

ul: A **spirit level** shows level and plumb. Check it by reading it on a surface, turning it end for end and reading it again: if the bubble sits in a different place, the level is out.
A **laser level** throws a level line or point round a room for box heights, trunking and tray runs.

An **angle finder** (digital inclinometer or protractor) reads an angle in degrees: the tilt of a solar panel frame, the slope of a roof for a bracket, or the angle of a conduit bend. Zero it on a surface you know is level, or as the maker says.

blocks.note: Solar PV frames are set to the tilt the designer gives. Use an angle finder on the frame itself: judging a tilt by eye, or by counting roof sheets, can be several degrees out.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A number without a unit is not a measurement. '1.5' could be 1.5 mm, 1.5 m or 1.5 mm². Record every reading with its **unit**, what was measured and where, the **device used and its number**, the date and your name. Then anyone can check it later, and if a device is found to be faulty, you can find every reading it gave.

flow: Stop further fixing until the error is understood
Re-measure a sample yourself to confirm the size of the error
Watch the person measure: datum, floor level, hook, eye position, pressure
Check their device against a good one
Explain the cause and show the right method
Correct the work, record what happened and check their next job

ul: Give every device its **own number** and list it in a **register**: type, range, where it is kept, the date of its last check, the result and when the next check is due. The number lets you trace each device's checks and faults.
Keep a **reference tape** (or rule) that is used only for checking the others and never for work, so it stays unworn. Compare each tape with it at several points along its length.
Check calipers and micrometers at zero, then against **gauge blocks** or setting standards at several sizes across their range.
Compare laser meters with the reference tape over known distances.
Check at **set times** (the Centre or company decides how often) and **after any knock or drop**.
Record the date, the readings, the error and who did the check.

blocks.p: A device outside the limits is **tagged and taken out of use** until it is adjusted, repaired or replaced. Do not keep using it 'with a correction' unless the maker's instructions and your supervisor allow it, and never bend a tape hook back with pliers and carry on. Then look back through the records: work measured with that device since its last good check may need checking again.

blocks.note: Reference standards themselves need checking against national standards from time to time. In Jamaica this is done by a calibration laboratory; the Bureau of Standards Jamaica offers calibration services. Your instructor will tell you how the Centre arranges it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Wipe each device clean and dry after use. Sweat, dust and salt air start rust within days.
Put a light film of oil on bare steel parts of rules, calipers and micrometers before storing them.
Keep each device in its own case, so that it is not knocked. Store a micrometer with its faces **slightly apart**, never screwed tight shut.
Wind tapes in slowly, guiding the blade, so the hook does not slam into the case. Dry a wet tape before winding it in.
Keep the lens of a laser meter clean and store it in its case. Take the batteries out if it will not be used for a long time, so they cannot leak.

Do not leave devices in a closed van or on a window ledge in the sun. Heat and damp affect accuracy, damage batteries and displays, and cause rust. In the van, keep them in a closed box, out of the sun, and secured so they do not rattle about.
Report any drop or damage at once. Hiding it puts wrong measurements into other people's work.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can convert between millimetres, metres, inches and feet, and between N·m and lb-in.
I can explain resolution, accuracy, tolerance and datum.
I can choose the right device for a cable route, a box height, a conductor diameter, a cable diameter, a gap, a depth, an angle and a terminal torque.
I can measure safely in and near electrical equipment, at height and with lasers.
I can use a steel tape, a fibreglass tape, a folding rule, a laser distance meter and a measuring wheel, and say what makes each read wrongly.
I can take lengths off a scaled drawing and explain the limits of doing so.
I can set heights from finished floor level, allowing for the floor finish.
I can set out from a datum and a level line, and space fittings evenly.
I can read a 0.02 mm vernier caliper and a 0.01 mm micrometer, and correct for a zero error.
I can find the size of a solid and a stranded conductor by measuring.
I can work out a minimum bend radius, the space cables take in a conduit, the number of fixings on a run and an order length.
I can set a torque tool and use a strip gauge, feeler gauges, a depth gauge and an angle finder.
I can record a measurement properly and check it against a tolerance.
I can find the cause when someone's measurements are wrong, and coach them.
I can check devices against a reference, keep the register and deal with a faulty device.
I can clean and store measuring devices in Jamaican conditions.

How close a reading is to the true size.
AFFL / FFL
Above finished floor level / finished floor level: the level of the floor after tiles or other finishes are laid.
Angle finder
A device that reads an angle or tilt in degrees; also called an inclinometer.
Anvil and spindle
The fixed and moving measuring faces of a micrometer.
AWG
American Wire Gauge: a conductor size system in which a lower number is a thicker wire.
Cross-sectional area
The area of the cut end of a conductor, in mm²; the conductor's 'size'.
Cumulative error
Error that builds up when each measurement starts from the last one.
Datum
The fixed point or line from which all positions are measured.
Feeler gauges
Thin blades of known thickness for measuring small gaps.
Gauge block
A precision block of exact size, used to check calipers and micrometers.
Laser distance meter
A device that measures distance with a laser beam.
Measuring wheel
A wheel with a counter, pushed along the ground to measure long distances.
Parallax error
A reading error from viewing a scale at an angle.
Ratchet
The part of a micrometer that slips at the right measuring pressure.
Reference tape
A tape kept only for checking other tapes, never used for work.
Register
The list of numbered devices with their checks, results and due dates.
Resolution
The smallest step a device can show.
Scale rule
A rule marked in drawing scales, for reading real lengths off a drawing.
Strip gauge
A mark on an accessory showing how much insulation to strip.
Tolerance
The allowed difference from the stated size, such as ± 5 mm.
Torque
Turning force, measured in newton metres (N·m).
Zero error
The reading a caliper or micrometer shows when it is closed and should read zero.

c1.title: Setting out a classroom in Bath
c1.text: Kerone Spencer, a Level 3 trainee, leads two trainees setting out a new classroom at a school in Bath, St Thomas. The drawing shows four ceiling lights in one row along the 8.4 m length of the room, with half a space at each end wall, outlets at 400 mm AFFL and switches at 1,200 mm AFFL. The floor is bare concrete; it will get 10 mm tiles on 20 mm of bedding. The team's copy of the 1:50 drawing was printed 'reduced to fit' on small paper.

c2.title: Unmarked cable at a Buff Bay farm store
c2.text: At a farm supply store in Buff Bay, Portland, Level 3 trainee Nadine Ellis is checking leftover, disconnected cable before any of it is used on a pump circuit. None of it is marked. Sample A has a solid copper conductor. Sample B has a stranded conductor with 7 strands. She has a 0–25 mm outside micrometer reading to 0.01 mm. With its clean faces closed by the ratchet, the micrometer reads −0.01 mm.

c3.title: Measuring a warehouse in Hayes
c3.text: Trainee Garth Wallace and his supervisor Ms Yanique Bailey are measuring a warehouse in Hayes, Clarendon, for a new cable tray. They have a 30 m fibreglass tape and a laser distance meter. Garth holds the back of the laser meter against one wall and reads 7.24 m to the opposite wall; the tape along the floor gives 7.36 m. The meter's body is 120 mm long. The roof steel is about 5.5 m above the floor, and one end of the building has a roller door open to bright sun.

c4.title: Device check day in Alexandria
c4.text: Trainee Shamoy Grant helps her instructor check the measuring devices at a training centre in Alexandria, St Ann. The reference tape was checked by a calibration laboratory this year. Against it, tape No. 7 reads 5,003 mm at 5,000 mm and tape No. 9 reads 5,001 mm. Caliper No. 3 reads 25.02 mm on a 25.00 mm gauge block. The Centre's limits are ± 2 mm at 5 m for tapes and ± 0.03 mm for calipers. The hook of tape No. 11 slides about 1 mm, which is its own thickness. Micrometer No. 2 was dropped yesterday and then used on a job.

c5.title: Cable for a villa in Whitehouse
c5.text: Trainee Kimani Lawrence is working out the cable for outdoor lighting at a villa in Whitehouse, Westmoreland. On the 1:200 site plan, the route from the board to the gazebo measures 64 mm. There are two drops of 1.5 m. He will add 10% for waste, and the supplier sells this cable by the foot. Part of the route is a 40 m trench line with two bends across a rough, stony garden. Three insulated conductors, each 4.2 mm in overall diameter, will go in a conduit where 80 mm² of cable area is allowed.

questions.q: At what height above the bare concrete should Kerone mark the outlet boxes?
o: 370 mm
400 mm
430 mm
410 mm
questions.why: Heights are given above finished floor level. The finish will add 10 + 20 = 30 mm, so the mark on the bare slab is 400 + 30 = 430 mm. Measuring 400 mm from the slab would leave every outlet 30 mm low once the tiles are laid.

questions.q: How far from the end wall is the centre of the first light?
questions.why: With half a space at each end, spacing = 8.4 ÷ 4 = 2.1 m, and the first light is half of that, 1.05 m, from the wall. Dividing by 5 (1.68 m) would give full spaces at the ends instead.

questions.q: One trainee marks each switch box by measuring from the box before it. What is likely to go wrong?
o: The tape hook will wear out more quickly
Small errors add up along the row
Each box will end up exactly 30 mm low
The boxes will be right, but slow to mark
questions.why: Each measurement carries the error of the one before, so the errors add up: this is cumulative error. Measuring every position from one datum, and heights from a level line, keeps each error on its own.

questions.q: The team's copy of the drawing was printed 'reduced to fit'. What does that mean for a distance Kerone needs?
o: He can scale it with the 1:100 edge of the scale rule
He should scale it at 1:50 and add 10% to be safe
He must use written dimensions, as the scale is lost
He should measure it on the print with a steel rule
questions.why: A reduced print is no longer at its stated scale, so anything scaled from it is wrong by an unknown amount. Use the written dimensions and ask the designer for any that are missing, or get a print at true size.

questions.q: On Sample A the sleeve shows 2.5 mm and the thimble shows 26. Allowing for the micrometer's zero error, what is the diameter?
questions.why: The reading is 2.50 + 0.26 = 2.76 mm. A closed reading of −0.01 mm means the micrometer reads 0.01 mm too small, so add it: 2.76 + 0.01 = 2.77 mm. A positive zero error would be subtracted instead.

questions.q: Nadine measures Sample A again at right angles and gets 2.71 mm. What does the difference between her two readings suggest?
o: The conductor is out of round at that spot
The micrometer's zero error has doubled since
The conductor is aluminium rather than copper
The ratchet is giving too little pressure
questions.why: A round conductor measures the same in every direction. A difference of 0.06 mm means it has been flattened or damaged at that spot, perhaps by pliers or a terminal screw. Measure again on an undamaged length before working out the area.

questions.q: One strand of Sample B measures 1.35 mm. What size is the conductor?
o: 1.5 mm²
6 mm²
16 mm²
10 mm²
questions.why: One strand = 3.142 × 1.35 × 1.35 ÷ 4 = 1.43 mm², and 7 strands = 7 × 1.43 = 10.0 mm². Measuring across the whole bundle would include the gaps between strands and give too large a size.

questions.q: On an undamaged part, Sample A measures a true 2.76 mm in both directions. Which standard size is it?
o: 4 mm²
2.5 mm²
6 mm²
10 mm²
questions.why: Area = π × d² ÷ 4 = 3.142 × 2.76 × 2.76 ÷ 4 = 5.98 mm², which is a 6 mm² conductor. The size is the area, not the diameter: a 2.76 mm conductor is not a '2.5'.

questions.q: The laser meter reads 7.24 m but the tape gives 7.36 m. What is the most likely cause?
o: The fibreglass tape has stretched by 120 mm
The meter is set to measure from its front edge
The warehouse is too warm for the laser to work
The laser's batteries are low, so it reads short
questions.why: The difference is exactly the length of the meter's body. Held with its back against the wall but set to measure from its front edge, the meter leaves out its own length. Check the reference setting on the display before every job.

questions.q: Which is the safest way for Garth to find the height from the floor to the underside of the roof steel?
o: Push the fibreglass tape up with a long broom handle
Climb a stepladder and stretch a tape up the rest of it
Count the wall's block courses and multiply by one block
Stand the laser meter on the floor, aimed straight up
questions.why: The laser meter measures the height from the floor, so nobody has to climb or over-reach. Rest it flat on the floor so the beam is vertical, and check that the dot is on the steel and not on a purlin or a light fitting.

questions.q: Garth and Ms Bailey hold the 30 m tape in the air across the building for the tray length, and it sags in the middle. What should they do?
o: Take 5% off the reading to allow for the sag
Pull as hard as they can until the tape is straight
Use the reading, as a sag makes very little difference
Lay the tape along the floor on the same line
questions.why: A sagging tape follows a curve, so it reads longer than the true straight distance, by an amount nobody can guess. Supporting the tape along the floor removes the sag. Pulling a fibreglass tape very hard stretches it and damages it.

questions.q: Near the roller door, the laser dot cannot be seen on the far wall in the bright sun. What helps most?
o: Use a target plate, or the meter's viewfinder
Hold a mirror on the wall to brighten the dot
Aim at a workmate's shirt instead of the wall
Take the reading anyway and add 10% to it
questions.why: If you cannot see the dot, you do not know what the meter measured to. A target plate or a viewfinder shows where the beam lands. A mirror could throw the beam into someone's eyes, and a laser is never aimed at a person.

questions.q: Which result means a device must be tagged and taken out of use?
o: Tape No. 9, reading 5,001 mm at 5,000 mm
Caliper No. 3, reading 25.02 mm at 25.00 mm
Tape No. 7, reading 5,003 mm at 5,000 mm
The reference tape, checked by a laboratory
questions.why: Tape No. 7 is 3 mm out, beyond the ± 2 mm limit. Tape No. 9 (1 mm out) and caliper No. 3 (0.02 mm out, limit ± 0.03 mm) are inside their limits. A device outside its limits is tagged, removed and recorded.

questions.q: Shamoy thinks tape No. 11 is faulty because its hook slides. What is the right judgement?
o: It is faulty: rivet the hook tight so that it cannot move
It is faulty: add 1 mm to every reading taken with it
It is fine for inside measurements, but not outside ones
It is fine: the hook is made to slide by its thickness
questions.why: The hook slides by its own thickness so that the tape reads correctly both when hooked over an edge and when pushed against a surface. A hook that is bent, stuck, or slides more than its thickness is the fault to look for.

questions.q: Micrometer No. 2 was dropped yesterday and then used on a job. What should happen now?
o: Check it on standards and review yesterday's readings
Carry on using it, as it still closes and reads zero
Oil the thread well and put it back in its case for now
Throw it away and write off the whole of yesterday's job
questions.why: A drop can bend the frame or damage the faces without it showing at zero, so the micrometer is checked across its range against gauge blocks or setting standards. If it is out, every reading taken since the drop is suspect and must be checked again.

questions.q: Why must the reference tape never be lent out for work on site?
o: It is too short to be of any use on a real job site
Wear or damage would make later checks wrong
It is marked in inches, which sites do not use
It belongs to the calibration laboratory, not us
questions.why: Every other tape is judged against the reference. If the reference is worn, kinked or stretched by site use, the checks pass bad tapes and fail good ones without anyone knowing. It is kept clean, cased and used only for checking.

questions.q: What is the real length of the route from the board to the gazebo?
questions.why: Real length = drawing length × scale number = 64 mm × 200 = 12,800 mm = 12.8 m. Check that an answer is sensible: 1.28 m would not cross a garden, and 128 m is longer than most plots.

questions.q: With the two drops and the 10% allowance, about how many feet of cable should Kimani order?
o: About 52 ft
About 190 ft
About 5.3 ft
About 57 ft
questions.why: 12.8 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 15.8 m. Adding 10%: 15.8 × 1.10 = 17.4 m. In feet: 17.4 ÷ 0.3048 = 57 ft. The 52 ft figure leaves out the waste allowance; 5.3 ft comes from multiplying by 0.3048 instead of dividing.

questions.q: About how much cable area do the three conductors take in the conduit?
o: About 14 mm²
About 166 mm²
About 25 mm²
About 42 mm²
questions.why: One conductor = 3.142 × 4.2 × 4.2 ÷ 4 = 13.9 mm², and three = 41.6 mm², well inside the 80 mm² allowed. The 166 mm² figure forgets to divide by 4. Use the overall diameter, including the insulation.

questions.q: Which method gives the most reliable length for the 40 m trench line across the rough, stony garden?
o: A measuring wheel pushed along the stony ground
A fibreglass tape laid along the route in stages
Pacing out the route and counting the steps taken
The laser meter aimed from one end to the other end
questions.why: A measuring wheel bounces and slips on rough, loose ground, and a laser measures only a straight line, not a route with bends. A long fibreglass tape laid along each straight part, with the parts added together, follows the real route.
